Abstract Background  A training program for intensive care unit (ICU) physicians entitled “Chinese Critical Care Certified Course” (5 C) started in China in 2009, intending to improve the quality of intensive care provision. This study aimed to explore the associations between the 5 C certification of physicians and the quality of intensive care provision in China. Methods  This nationwide analysis collected data regarding 5 C-certified physicians between 2009 and 2019. Fifteen ICU quality control indicators (three structural, four procedural, and eight outcome-based) were collected from the Chinese National Report on the Services, Quality, and Safety in Medical Care System. Provinces were stratified into three groups based on the cumulative number of 5 C certified physicians per million population. Results  A total of 20,985 (80.41%) physicians from 3,425 public hospitals in 30 Chinese provinces were 5 C certified. The deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis rate in the high 5 C physician-number provinces was significantly higher than in the intermediate 5 C physician-number provinces (67.6% vs. 55.1%, p = 0.043), while ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) rate in the low 5 C physician-number provinces was significantly higher than in the high 5 C physician-number provinces (14.9% vs. 8.9%, p = 0.031). Conclusions  The higher number of 5 C-certified physicians per million population seemed to be associated with higher DVT prophylaxis rates and lower VAP rates in China, suggesting that the 5 C program might have a beneficial impact on the quality of intensive care provision. Keywords  Chinese Critical Care Certified Course, Intensive Care Unit Training, Training Program, Healthcare Improvement, Critical Care, Continuous Training

# Chinese critical care certified course in intensive care unit: a nationwide-based analysis

Background Intensive care units (ICUs) provide specialized treatment for several serious life-threatening injuries and condi­ tions, aiming to deliver continual day-to-day care with high-skill personnel and expert equipment. ICU physi­ cians are required to make instantaneous decisions [1, 2] which may directly determine the patients’ survival. Despite constant improvements, medical errors or lowerquality of intensive care provision are still observed in 27-58% of ICU admissions [3] and are associated with higher ICU mortality [4].

Early diagnosis and intervention were shown to deter­ mine the prognosis of critical diseases such as sepsis, respiratory failure, or COVID-19 [5, 6]. Therefore, con­ tinuous training for ICU physicians in multiple disci­ plines is likely to improve their abilities to manage critical clinical conditions. The principle of formal up-to-date ongoing training is applied worldwide as one of the important ways to improve the quality of ICU medical care and reduce the mortality of the critically ill popula­ tion [7–9]. Although some such training programs have been successfully utilized in sepsis or HIV/AIDS, there is still room for further improvement [10, 11].

In 2009 the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine and the Organization Management Department, and the Department of Continuing Education created a training model to standardize ICU care based on the American Society of Critical Care Medicine FCCS course (https:// www.sccm.org/Fundamentals/Fundamental-Critical- Care-Support), the American Heart Association ECC course (https://cpr.heart.org/en), and the China Taiwan ACLS Joint Committee Courses (http://www.tsccm. org.tw/English/eng002.asp). The training program was named “Chinese Critical Care Certified Course (5  C)” (Supplementary File 1). For a decade (2009–2019), this program enrolled almost 20,000 clinicians in 31 prov­ inces in China and provided multidisciplinary teams for training in an attempt to decrease ICU mortality [6, 12]. Our previous study reported that the increasing number of 5 C physicians was linked to lower COVID mortality [6], while another study reported controversial results for overall mortality [13]. The intended and actual effects of the 5  C certification program on other indicators of hospital care provision quality remain to be further discussed.

Based on the above, this study aimed to explore the associations between the 5 C certification of physicians and the quality of intensive care provision in China, focusing on the ICU quality indicators from Chinese national reports and analyzing its association with the number of 5 C physicians per million population.

Methods Study design This nationwide analysis enrolled physicians who par­ ticipated in the Chinese 5 C training program (5 C phy­ sicians) between 2009 and 2019; ICU quality indicators were collected across China between 2015 and 2018. This study was approved by the Ethnic Committee of Zheji­ ang Hospital. Informed consent was waived by the Ethnic Committee due to the retrospective study design.

5 C training The training consists of theoretical training and skill training. The theoretical training includes identification and assessment of severe patients, basic principles and methods of severe patient monitoring, hemodynamic monitoring and correction methods, shock, cardiopul­ monary cerebral resuscitation, respiratory failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and critical asthma, acute respiratory distress syndrome, mechanical ventilation, mechanical ventilation-related technologies, diagnosis and treatment of severe cardiovascular diseases, diag­ nosis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmo­ nary embolism hemorrhage and coagulation disorders in severe patients, application principles of antibiotics in the ICU, fungal infection, catheter-related bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, sepsis and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, acute liver injury and acute liver failure in severe patients, gastrointestinal failure in severe patients, enteral and parenteral nutri­ tion support in severe patients, diagnosis and treatment of acute kidney injury, severe blood purification technol­ ogy, analgesia and sedation of critically ill patients, criti­ cal diagnosis and treatment of central nervous system, internal environment disorder of critically ill patients, endocrine parameters and metabolism of critically ill patients, trauma, and scientific research in intensive care medicine. The skill training includes artificial airway establishment, mechanical ventilation, placement of vas­ cular catheters, hemodynamic monitoring, and continu­ ous renal replacement therapy techniques. The training is delivered face-to-face. The entire training duration is 4 days. The average size of an ICU is 20 beds, and they usually work as closed ICUs. Monthly classes can be held nationwide, in one place at a time. According to the offi­ cial website of the Intensive Care Medicine Branch of the Chinese Medical Association, the website enrollment brochure, and online registration, the students choose their own time and location, at their convenience, to receive training and assessment.

Data collection and definition Data regarding the 5  C physicians were collected from the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine between 2009 and 2019, including their hospital, department,

and province. A 5 C physician was defined as a clinician who had completed 5 C training and received 5 C certi­ fication. Since the ICU quality control survey in China was initiated in 2015, quality indicators between 2016 and 2018 were collected (including three structural, four procedural, and eight outcome-based) from the National Report on the Services, Quality, and Safety in Medical Care System issued by the National Health Commission of the People’s Republic of China. Specifically, the struc­ tural indicators were (1) the proportion of ICU patients to the total number of inpatients, (2) the proportion of ICU bed occupancy to the total inpatient bed occupancy, and (3) the proportion of patients with Acute Physiol­ ogy, and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) [14] II scores ≥ 15 to all ICU patients. The procedural indicators were (1) the 3-h Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) bundle compliance rate [15], (2) the 6-h SSC bundle compliance rate [15], (3) the microbiology detection rate before anti­ biotics, and (4) deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis rate. The outcome-based indicators were (1) unplanned endotracheal extubation rate, (2) reintubation rate within 48 h, (3) unplanned ICU transfer rate, (4) ICU readmis­ sion rate within 48 h, (5) ventilator-associated pneumo­ nia (VAP) rate, (6) catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) rate, (7) catheter-associated urinary tract infec­ tion (CAUTI) rate, and (8) ICU mortality.

Population demographic data were derived from the 2020 China National Population Census, and provinces were stratified based on the cumulative number of 5 C physicians per million population and then divided into tertiles (three groups: low, intermediate, and high 5  C physician-number provinces). As the authors worked in Zhejiang province and data from many physicians were available in Zhejiang, data in Zhejiang province were subanalyzed. Hospitals in Zhejiang were stratified according to the ratio of the number of physicians to ICU beds per hospital into 2 subgroups.

The gross domestic product (GDP) data in each prov­ ince (except Taiwan) in China were collected from the China Statistical Yearbooks from the National Bureau of Statistics of the People’s Republic of China (available at: http://www.stats.gov.cn/tjsj/ndsj). Provinces were strati­ fied according to GDP into 2 subgroups. The 5 C physi­ cian data and ICU quality indicators were compared in provinces with different GDPs and areas.

Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed utilizing SPSS 22.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) and GraphPad Prism 6 (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). Con­ tinuous variables with a normal distribution (accord­ ing to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) were described as means ± standard deviations and were compared with the independent sample Student t-test between two groups

or compared using one-way analysis of variance among three groups; continuous variables with skewed distri­ butions were described as medians (quartiles) and were compared using Mann-Whitney U test between two groups or with Kruskal-Wallis H test and post hoc analy­ sis among three groups. The categorical variables were described as n (%) and analyzed using the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. The correlation between the cumula­ tive number of 5 C certified physicians per million popu­ lation and ICU quality indicators in each province was evaluated using the Spearman correlation analysis. All tests were two-sided, and p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Results 5 C certified physicians One hundred twenty-eight training sessions were held in the 5 C training program between 2009 and 2019 with 26,099 physicians. The top three provinces with the high­ est number of 5 C physicians were Henan (9.59%), Jiangsu (8.63%), and Guangdong (6.99%), while Qinghai, Hainan, and Ningxia provinces had the fewest (Fig.  1a). As of 2019, a total of 20,985 physicians (80.41%) were 5 C certi­ fied, and the number of 5 C certified physicians trained each subsequent year has been steadily increasing, from 603 to 2009 to 3312 in 2019 (Fig. 1b); the passing rates varied from 72.7 to 90.5%. The top three provinces with the highest number of 5  C physicians per provincial population were Xinjiang, Gansu, and Hainan (Fig. 1c). A total of 13,158 (62.7%) of the 5 C-certified physicians worked in tertiary hospitals. In total, 15,319 5 C-certified physicians (73.0%) were working in the ICU department.

Associations of 5 C certified physicians and ICU quality A total of 3,425 ICUs reported quality indicators. There was no significant correlation between the cumulative number of 5 C certified physicians per million population and ICU quality indicators in each province (Data not shown). The DVT prophylaxis rate in the high 5 C phy­ sician-number provinces was significantly higher than in the intermediate 5 C physician-number provinces (67.6% vs. 55.1%, p = 0.043), and the VAP rate in the low 5 C phy­ sician-number provinces was significantly higher than in the high 5 C physician-number provinces (14.9% vs. 8.9%, p = 0.031) (Table 1).

Changes in ICU quality The cumulative number of 5  C certified physicians per million population has increased significantly from 7.8 (6.5, 12.7) in 2016 to 14.4 (9.9, 19.3) in 2018 (Table 2). The microbiology detection rate before antibiotics has also shown a significant increase from 70.52% (65.2%, 74.1%) in 2016 to 79.72% (78.29%, 83.8%) in 2018 (p < 0.001). 5 C-certified physicians and ICU quality in different areas There was no significant difference in the number of 5 C certified physicians per million population between the low-GDP provinces [10.8 (7.2, 12.5)] and high-GDP provinces [9.1 (8.2, 17.0)] (p = 0.694), and ICU quality indicators were similar between the 2 subgroups (Supple­ mentary Table S1). The median number of 5 C certified physicians per million population in the east, northeast, southwest, northwest, and central areas of China per province were 1.3 (0.8–1.8), 0.7 (0.7–0.8), 1.5 (1.1–2.2), 0.9 (0.9–1.4) and 0.6 (0.6–0.8), respectively, with signifi­ cant difference (p = 0.029) (Supplementary Table S2). The VAP rates in the east, northeast, southwest, northwest, and central areas of China per province were signifi­ cantly different (9.15% vs. 15.00% vs. 15.26% vs. 8.90% vs. 14.75%, p = 0.041) (Supplementary Table S2).

Discussion Intensive care medicine in China has the same disciplin­ ary status as internal medicine and surgery, which belong to secondary disciplines. After obtaining the physician qualification, physicians planning to work in the ICU should receive the 5 C training and a qualification certifi­ cate. The present study revealed a significant association between the higher numbers of 5 C certified physicians per million population and a higher DVT prophylaxis

rate, as well as a lower VAP rate, highlighting the impor­ tance of the nationwide 5 C training program for improv­ ing the critical care provision quality.

In 2017, the World Health Organization recognized the value of training initiatives as a global health priority, highlighting its importance in improving care outcomes [16]. It has been reported that proper training, more reliable ultrasound, and clinical microbiology practices are essential for the early detection of sepsis [5, 17]. In this study, the 3-h SSC bundles compliance and 6-h SSC bundles compliance did not differ between the provinces with the different numbers of 5 C physicians per popu­ lation (all p > 0.05). It could be partly explained by the comparable microbiology detection rate before antibiot­ ics (p > 0.05) and other general characteristics. However, this analysis focused only on the qualification of the ICU physicians and did not consider the qualification and experience of the ICU nurses. Indeed, the experience of ICU nurses has been associated with the development of ICU sepsis [18]. In particular, Yousefi et al. [8] evalu­ ated nurses’ knowledge before and after training, demon­ strating improved quality of sepsis care. Nonetheless, the DVT prophylaxis rate was gradually increasing with the increase in the number of 5 C physicians per population, with a significant > 10% difference between the interme­ diate and high provinces, suggesting that better training of physicians is conducive to the individualization of clin­ ical practice and might potentially lead to better sepsis and DVT outcomes.

Multidisciplinary knowledge is key to successful ICU pneumonia prevention [12]. Previous studies have con­ firmed that implementing robust multidisciplinary train­ ing improves overall intensive care provision quality [19, 20] and has been proven effective in optimizing the quality of anesthesia-associated care in particular [21, 22]. Of note, ICU teams led by intensivists or physicians trained in critical care have been shown to improve VAP outcomes [23, 24]. In line with the above research, this study demonstrated that the cumulative number of 5 C certified physicians per million population has increased almost two-fold between 2016 and 2018, while the VAP rate has decreased; with that VAP rate in the provinces with the low tertile number of 5 C physicians was almost 1.5 higher than in the high 5 C physician-number prov­ inces. Prevention of VAP is the focus in ICU, especially for immunocompromised patients, older adults, and postoperative patients [25]. Obtained results suggest that 5 C training improves physicians’ knowledge and skills, leading to enhanced team performance that might pre­ vent VAP with higher success.

Although adequate personnel training is vital for the successful management of the ICU, a previous study, fin­ ished in 2020 [13], failed to find an association between 5  C training and the reduction of ICU mortality. Cur­ rently, 5 C is the only national professional qualification training program in China that introduces standardized textbooks and standard courseware in clinical medicine, providing a continuing education model for other dis­ ciplines. The program is based on theoretical training taught in modules through theoretical key points, case discussions, questions and answers, and skill training. Some improvements are discussed based on the results of this study, including the revision of the 5 C textbook. The teaching PowerPoint has been continuously improved and revised to form an exceptional standardized course component. The form of theoretical training is more diversified and includes case discussions with questions, with answers added to the initial theoretical teaching. Conversely, physicians’ feedback can help improve the program and should be considered, while additional training methods should be explored for the next revision of the 5 C program, including the simulation-based train­ ing that recently demonstrated satisfactory results [26].

One of the goals for improving national medical quality and safety in 2022 and 2023 is to increase the standard­ ized prevention rate of venous thromboembolism. The core strategy is as follows: (1) Medical institutions should establish a VTE prevention and control system within the hospital, a VTE management team composed of medi­ cal, clinical, nursing, and other departments, develop a scientific VTE prevention and control management path and carry out standardized VTE risk assessment and pre­ vention. (2) Information technology should be used to

strengthen VTE prevention reminders, data collection, monitoring, and evaluation feedback of quality control indicators and incorporate them into performance man­ agement, establishing incentive and constraint mecha­ nisms. (3) Effective mass management tools should be used to find and analyze the factors that affect the organi­ zation to achieve this goal and to propose and implement continuous improvement measures. (4) VTE-related consultation, referral mechanisms, and emergency plans should be designed to achieve the treatment and man­ agement of severe VTE patients. (5) The hospital should implement VTE prevention and control technology guid­ ance, teaching training, and related exchanges to improve VTE awareness and standardized prevention and control capabilities.

A major strength of the present study is its nation­ wide design and large sample size. This study covered the 11-year consecutive annual 5 C training data in 30 prov­ inces (except Hong Kong, Macao, Xizang, and Taiwan) in China and data from the National Report of ICU qual­ ity control indicators. In addition, this is the first study to explore the impact of the cumulative number of 5 C-cer­ tified physicians on ICU quality to date, and the results are noteworthy as they highlighted the beneficial role of the nationwide 5 C training program on ICU quality improvement.

However, the present study is not without limitations. Firstly, the study was conducted based on generalized hospital data, not specific patient-based data. Secondly, the 5 C physicians were not evaluated for their individual knowledge and skills in critical care, and only the certi­ fication rate was available. Thirdly, the quality control indicators of the unit of each physician and the patients treated cannot correspond in a one-to-one way. In addi­ tion, some participating hospitals had very low numbers of physicians, which could lead to non-different out­ comes in those hospitals. Fourthly, an interesting decline in CRBSI was observed between 2016 and 2018, but the reasons can be very complex (e.g., strengthened hospital infection prevention, improved maintenance of venous catheters, improved training, etc.), and the available data for the present study do not allow determining the exact reasons. Finally, the effect of the 5 C physicians may not be immediate and require long-term evaluation.

An important point to underline is that the present study demonstrates the difficulties inherent in evaluating a complex intervention like the 5 C educational program regarding its downstream effects on a large population of ICU patients. One of the strategies used here was to stratify the hospitals into tertiles of the proportion of 5  C-certified physicians to evaluate the intervention effect. Still, as shown in Table  1, even these propor­ tions within tertiles are not significantly different from each other (P = 0.107). If, at the outset, the proportion

Conclusions Provinces with a higher number of 5 C certified physi­ cians per million population seem to be associated with higher DVT prophylaxis rates and lower VAP rates in China, suggesting that the 5 C program might have a ben­ eficial impact on the quality of intensive care provision.

# Renal hemodynamic evaluation protocol based on the pathophysiological mechanism of acute kidney injury: Critical Care UltraSound Guided-A(KI)BCDE

**Authors:** Lixia Liu; Dawei Liu; Zhenjie Hu; Xiaoting Wang; Yangong Chao; Jun Wu; Wanhong Yin; Hongmin Zhang; Lina Zhang; Wei He; Ran Zhu; Qianghong Xu; Rongli Yang; Yan Huo; Qian Zhang; Haitao Liu; Weihua Zhu; Qian Zhang; Rong Li

## Abstract

The multiple etiological characteristics of acute kidney injury (AKI) have brought great challenges to its clinical diagnosis and treatment. Renal injury in critically ill patients always indicates hemodynamic injury. The Critical Care UltraSound Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol developed by the Chinese Critical Ultrasound Study Group (CCUSG), respectively, includes A(KI) diagnosis and risk assessment and uses B-mode ultrasound, Color doppler ultrasound, spectral Doppler ultrasound, and contrast Enhanced ultrasound to obtain the hemodynamic characteristics of the kidney so that the pathophysiological mechanism of the occurrence and progression of AKI can be captured and the prognosis of AKI can be predicted combined with other clinical information; therefore, the corresponding intervention and treatment strategies can be formulated to achieve targeted, protocolized, and individualized therapy.

## Background

Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in more than half of critically ill patients and is an independent risk factor for poor prognosis. AKI is a complex clinical syndrome encompassing a wide spectrum of etiologies, such as sepsis, volume depletion, inflammation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, exogenous and endogenous toxins, surgery, obstruction, heart failure, and others. These various triggers often coexist in one patient simultaneously, therefore making it very challenging to identify the etiologies and relevant therapeutic targets. The current diagnostic criteria, biomarkers [1–3], and electronic alarming systems [4,5] are not appropriately used in identifying the etiology of AKI and guiding the treatment.

A series of studies have confirmed that renal hemodynamic alterations in critically ill patients is an independent risk factor for the occurrence and progression of AKI [6–10]. Thanks to the advantage of perfect morphological integration, the function of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and the availability of smaller and cost-effective ultrasound machines, the combination of evidence collected can better equip the non-radiologists and non-cardiologists, making them more competent in performing POCUS; therefore, this method is currently applied in many clinical settings and in all phases of care—from screening and diagnosis to procedural guidance and monitoring; its application has been associated with the changes in clinical decision making in medical practice [11,12]. Professional societies such as the International Liaison Committee on Lung Ultrasound [13], the American Society of Echocardiography [14], and the Chinese Critical Ultrasound Study Group (CCUSG) [15,16] have established guidelines on the use of POCUS; thus, POCUS will be used as a standard diagnostic tool for all clinicians [17]. The CCUSG developed a Critical-Care UltraSound Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol (Figure 1); using proven ultrasonic techniques, including two-dimensional (2D) ultrasound, doppler ultrasound and contrast-enhanced ultrasound, the renal anatomical structure and renal blood perfusion were evaluated to obtain comprehensive renal hemodynamic information, as well as the pathophysiological mechanisms of the occurrence and progression of AKI. Under critical ultrasound guidance [15], targeted and protocolized management can be implemented. This article aimed to describe in detail the method of implementing the CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol, which can provide support and guidance for clinicians, reduce the occurrence of AKI, and improve the prognosis of patients with AKI.

*Figure 1.: Critical Care UltraSound-Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol. AKI: acute kidney injury; MAP: mean arterial pressure; CO: cardiac output; IAP: intra-abdominal pressure; CVP: Central venous pressure.*

## AKI diagnosis and risk assessment of AKI occurrence and progression

Identifying AKI and determining the risk factors for its occurrence and progression is the initial step.

### Diagnosis of AKI

AKI is diagnosed according to the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines [1].

### Present and past history of illness

Present illness such as sepsis, shock, major bleeding, and acute cardiac failure and recent surgeries (e.g., cardiothoracic surgery and upper abdominal surgery), as well as past illnesses like hypertension and diabetes and long-term use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, chronic cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and renal replacement therapy (RRT) can all lead to the occurrence and progression of AKI by impairment of renal hemodynamics through various mechanisms [18].

## B-mode ultrasound

Organ structure determines organ function.

### Examination method

A convex probe with a frequency of 2.5–5 MHz is typically used. The examination is performed based on two basic planes (coronal plane and transverse plane) (Figure 2A,B). It includes size (length, width, thickness), internal measurements (parenchyma thickness, cortex thickness, and tubular inner diameter in the collective system), echogenicity (cortex, medulla, and collective system), and others (stone, tumor, cyst, abscess, and so on).

*Figure 2.: Two-dimensional ultrasonography of the kidneys. (A) Ultrasound image of a normal kidney, coronal plane. (B) Ultrasound image of a normal kidney, transverse plane. (C) Ultrasonography of acute kidney injury (AKI): a 59-year-old man, on the third day after Colon cancer surgery, had an abdominal infection and sepsis-associated AKI. The two-dimensional ultrasonography showed a slight increase in renal volume, parenchymal thickening, and increased cortical echogenicity. (D) Ultrasonography of chronic kidney disease (CKD): an 85-year-old woman with chronic renal insufficiency, severe pneumonia, heart failure, and AKI—a complication of CKD; the two-dimensional ultrasound indicated a significant reduction in the kidney volume, thinning of the parenchyma, blurry structure of the cortex and medulla, and increased cortical echogenicity. E. Ultrasonography of hydronephrosis: a 47-year-old woman with extensive metastases in the peritoneal cavity from ovarian cancer, right ureter compression, ureteral obstruction, renal pelvis dilation, and renal cortex thinning. F. Ultrasound image of the kidney cyst: a 69-year-old woman with AKI after rectal tumor surgery; polycystic kidney disease was diagnosed 12 years ago, and two-dimensional ultrasound showed multiple hypoechoic thin-walled cysts in the kidney.*

### Normal 2D ultrasonography

The normal ultrasound image is shown in Figure 2A. The kidneys are oval. Adult kidneys have a long axis diameter of 9–12 cm, a width of 5–7 cm, and a thickness of 4–5 cm. The parenchyma and cortex thickness are about 1–2 cm and 0.8–1 cm respectively. The cortex is equal-echo or slightly less than hepatic echo, while the medulla is hypoecho. The border between the cortex and medulla is relatively clear. Renal sinus accounts for about 1/2–2/3 of the kidney with hyper and heterogeneous echo. A tubular liquid dark area with a diameter of <1 cm may be seen within the sinus (Figure 2A).

### Pathophysiological and clinical significance of renal morphology

In some degree, the kidney volume, especially the thickness of the renal parenchyma reflects the numbers of functional nephrons. The fewer normal nephrons, the more impairment of renal function regardless of the subtypes of AKI. Volume enlargement and parenchymal thickening with increased echogenicity are often suggestive of acute lesions (Figure 2C). On the contrary, reduced volume and thinned parenchyma with increased echogenicity are often suggestive of chronic lesions (Figure 2D).

Three-dimensional ultrasound method such as Crislip GR [19] was used to evaluate the renal volume of rats with various durations of ischemia-reperfusion injury; results showed that ischemic durations of 15, 30, and 45 min resulted in a graded increase in kidney volume (Ptime 0.001) with a positively linear correlation between renal volume and the degree of renal tubular injury, which was superior to serum creatinine in terms of detection capability. In a small study of 26 patients with acute tubular necrosis, Nomura and others [20] demonstrated that the kidney size, especially the anteroposterior diameter, were positively correlated with serum creatinine and length of hospitalization. Cortical thickness and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) are well correlated with the stage of CKD and can be used to evaluate the phase and progression of CKD [21,22].

It should be pointed out that an abnormal kidney morphology mostly indicates renal histological and function disorders; however, a normal morphology under 2D ultrasonography does not necessarily indicate a healthy kidney; many patients with AKI present normal kidney volume, thickness, and echogenicity under conventional 2D ultrasonography.

## Color doppler ultrasound

Organ blood flow perfusion guarantees organ function, which is especially true of the kidneys [23].

Renal Blood Flow (RBF) accounts for 20%–25% of CO. RBF is not aimed at achieving self-survival but cleansing the metabolic wastes; regulating water, electrolyte, and acid-base; maintaining homeostasis; and regulating blood pressure and other important functions. Decreased renal blood perfusion suggests a reduction in the volume of blood that is filtrated, metabolized, and regulated by the kidneys; it is manifested as a disorder in the water, electrolyte, and acid-base balance, etc. When a certain level is reached, it is clinically defined as AKI. Color doppler flow mapping can intuitively display the conditions of renal blood perfusion, including the amount and the area of perfusion.

However, we need to note that although renal blood perfusion is a guarantee of kidney function, it is not the only factor determining kidney function, such as septic AKI is a typical representative [6,24]. Because the pathogenesis of septic AKI determines that renal blood perfusion is different in different periods, which may be normal or even increased in the early stage, and may be reduced in the late stage, with or without the redistribution from the medulla to cortex, which is also related to the severity of septic AKI In fact, all other types of AKI have similar characteristics, that is, the primary disease will lead to a certain degree of damage to the kidney itself, that is, blood perfusion is the fundamental guarantee, but it is not the only factor [6] In addition, due to the individual differences of each patient, even in the face of the same pathogenic factor, each patient’s response will be different, AKI performance will be different, and blood ­perfusion will be different. This is why we recommend a comprehensive evaluation, including both macro- and microcirculation [25].

### Examination method

Based on 2D ultrasound, color doppler mode is used.

### Normal color doppler ultrasound image

On normal color doppler ultrasound, the renal blood is observed flowing directly from the renal hilum to the renal cortex, filled the kidney (Figure 3D).

*Figure 3.: Semi-quantitative grading of renal blood flow distribution. (A) Grade 0, there is no blood flow to the kidneys. (B) Grade 1, a small volume of blood is flowing to the renal hilum. (C) Grade 2, most parts of the renal parenchyma are filled with blood. (D) Grade 3, the renal parenchyma is filled with blood. White arrow, interlobar artery. White arrowhead, interlobar vein.*

### Semi-quantitative grading of RBF distribution and its clinical application

The renal blood flow is classified into four grades: Grade 0, no blood flow in the kidney (Figure 3A); Grade 1, a small volume of blood flow in the renal hilum (Figure 3B); Grade 2, blood flowing to most parts of the renal parenchyma (Figure 3C); and Grade 3, normal renal blood flow to the cortex, filled (Figure 3D). This classification not only directly shows the renal blood perfusion, but can also be used to predict the occurrence of AKI within 24 h [26,27].

## Spectral doppler ultrasound

To a certain extent, the renal arteriovenous doppler waveforms and the corresponding renal resistive index (RRI) and venous impedance index (VII) can reflect the pathophysiological mechanisms and etiology of renal disease, guide treatment, and predict the prognosis.

### Renal artery assessment

#### Examination method

Steps: The probe with a frequency of 2.5–5 MHz is selected. The kidney’s maximum coronal section is obtained in 2D mode. Color Doppler is used to identify the renal intrarenal artery. The interlobar artery which walks through the renal column is located (Figure 3D). Pulse Doppler is selected, and the sampling line is placed on the blood flow, parallel to the blood flow as much as possible. Approximately 2–5 mm of the sample is acquired, and 3 to 5 similar consecutive waveforms are obtained in one breathing cycle. The peak systolic velocity rate and end diastolic velocity rate are measured in every 3 waveforms. The RRI is calculated as follows: RRI = (peak systolic velocity minus end diastolic velocity divided by peak systolic velocity. Then, the mean value is selected. The contralateral kidney is examined to obtain the RRI.

#### Renal artery waveform type and RRI

There are three types of renal artery waveform. The normal has a typical low resistance pattern, which is characterized by a rapid increase in systolic blood flow velocity and a slow decline in the diastolic phase. The diastolic flow velocity is 30%–50% of the systolic flow velocity with an RRI value of 0.5–0.7 (Figure 4A). The small slow wave (Figure 4B) indicates that the blood flow velocity is slow during systole and diastole, and a high resistance wave can be manifested as a rapid increase in the blood flow velocity during systole, and a quick drop or even disappearance of blood flow during diastole (Figure 4C,D). Both small slow wave and high-resistance wave are abnormal spectra, with RRI value of <0.5 and >0.7, respectively.

*Figure 4.: Waveform of renal arterial blood flow. (A) Normal renal interlobar artery waveform and renal resistance index value. (B) Small slow wave: a 37-year-old woman, a significant decrease in renal artery blood supply caused by aortic dissection; the blood flow in the proximal left renal artery from the abdominal aorta was almost interrupted; the distal wave of the interrupted blood flow showed a slow rise during systole, decreased peak value, and gradual decrease during diastole. (C–E) High-resistance wave: images shown in (B,C) are captured from the same patient. (C) shows the significantly reduced renal blood flow and a high-resistance waveform from the renal segmental artery; (D) shows a 31-year-old man with acute severe pancreatitis complicated with intra-abdominal hypertension and acute kidney injury, an intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) of 25 mmHg, and a nail-shaped waveform from the renal segmental artery, with diastolic blood flow interruption. The image shown in (E) is captured from the same patient. (E) shows the renal artery blood flow spectrum when IAP reduced to 12 mmHg after continuous renal replacement therapy. Compared with (D), (E) shows an increase in the peak systolic flow velocity, visible diastolic blood flow but significantly reduced blood flow velocity during diastole compared with that during systole, and a high-resistance waveform.*

#### Generation principle and influencing factors of renal artery waveform and RRI

Arterial Doppler waveform analysis is based on the changes in blood flow velocity caused by pulsatile arterial perfusion. The ratio of diastolic to systolic blood velocity is mainly determined based on the downstream resistance [28]. As resistance increases, the diastolic velocity decreases compared with the systolic velocity. However, the correlation between RRI and vascular resistance was influenced by multiple factors; thus, the use of RRI to guide blood pressure titration in shock patients was limited, among which vascular compliance, pulse pressure (PP), renal interstitial pressure, and distal vascular bed area are the main influential factors [29,30].

Vascular compliance directly determines the influence of resistance on RRI. The higher the compliance, the more the RRI was affected by resistance. In the absence of compliance, the RRI was independent of vascular resistance [31]. Age is a common factor affecting compliance, both younger and older age can lead to decreased vascular compliance. The RRI was ≥0.70 in patients aged ≤4 years. The RRI increases with age, especially in individuals aged 40 years and older [29,32,33]. Hypertension and diabetes often lead to decreased renal artery compliance, which may not affect the baseline RRI values, but reduce the RRI response to MAP changes in these patients [34]. Further increases in MAP may not confer additional benefit due to the reduced RRI response to MAP [35]. Renal interstitial pressure essentially reflects renal vascular compliance (the pressure difference between the intrarenal vessels and extrarenal vessels); renal interstitial pressure is positively correlated with RRI.

RRI increases as the cross-sectional area of the distal arterial bed decreases, and this effect is independent of the vascular compliance and RRI.

#### Clinical application of renal artery waveform and RRI

A comprehensive understanding of the generation principle and influencing factors of renal artery waveform and RRI is the basic premise for their appropriate clinical application, which needs to be integrated with the hemodynamic assessment of renal veins, renal microcirculation, and the body’s systemic circulations; empirical application often leads to unsatisfactory clinical outcomes.

#### Identify the etiologies

#### Small slow waveform: an RRI of <0.5

The main mechanism for its formation is the significant reduction in blood flow. It occurs more often in downstream of the remarkably narrow segment of the extrarenal artery and less often in the intrarenal arteries, especially the arterioles (Figure 4B). Obstruction removal is the key therapeutic strategy.

#### High-resistance waveform: an RRI of >0.7

The main mechanism for its formation is high blood flow resistance. Unlike small slow waveform, it occurs more frequently in the intrarenal arteries and the upstream of the remarkably narrow segment of the extrarenal artery. The common pathophysiological mechanisms in critically ill patients are renal vasoconstriction caused by renal hypoperfusion, decreased vascular compliance caused by increased renal interstitial pressure, and decreased distal vascular bed area caused by microcirculation disorders. The common etiologies are sepsis, cardiac dysfunction, hypovolemia, hypervolemia, inflammatory response, high intra-abdominal pressure, etc.

#### Titrate blood pressure

Titrate the optimal MAP by adjusting the dose of the vasopressors, and then select the MAP with the lowest RRI.

Although a number of factors influence the correlation between RRI and vascular resistance, MAP still has a positive correlation with RRI [36–38]. Remember that other causes of increased RRI should be addressed prior to MAP titration as far as possible since high dosages of norepinephrine can potentially cause cardiomyocyte damage, oxidative stress, and sepsis-related immunosuppression [39]. Certainly, vasopressors can be adjusted at the same time when the problem cannot be resolved immediately.

An elevated MAP may also lead to overperfusion in other organs, such as the cerebrum, especially when the autonomic regulation of cerebral blood flow is impaired [40]. At this time, the cerebral perfusion must be evaluated.

#### Guide fluid resuscitation

If the RRI is reduced after fluid resuscitation, it makes sense to resuscitate, otherwise it may increase the risk of fluid overload.

The goal of fluid resuscitation is to improve tissue perfusion by increasing CO and MAP, while the dissociation between the systemic and the renal response to fluid challenge was notable. Moussa et al. showed that fluid administration can result in a small but consistent decrease in RI, which were better predictors of an increase in urine output than were MAP and PP [41]. Ferré et al. also showed similar results. They found that a fluid challenge can decrease RRI in suspected hypovolaemia patients at risk of postoperative AKI, but the changes are not correlated to changes in CO [42]. While Schnell et al. did not find the same results, which would be due to the definition of the fluid responsiveness they used. They used an increase in descending aortic blood flow, a systemic response, to define the response of fluid challenge [43].

#### RRT management

In AKI, when RRI is <0.7, RRT not likely required; if RRI remains at ≥0.7 even after conventional treatment [44], which means that the renal pathophysiological status and function might not improve [44] and RRT is likely to be initiated. During RRT, a decreased RRI indicates a better prognosis. When the RRI is <0.7, successful discontinuation of RRT is highly likely. If the RRI remains ≥0.7 despite the recovery of renal function and successful discontinuation of RRT, which indicates that the renal pathological state has not been completely corrected. Hemodynamic instability is a common phenomenon during RRT and is associated with poor prognosis [45,46]. Hypotension occurring within 1 h after initiation of Continuous RRT (CRRT) is an independent risk factor for poor prognosis [46]. The RRI helps guide MAP setting [36–38], fluid resuscitation and volume management [41,42].

#### Predict the prognosis

Many studies have confirmed the predictive utility of RRI in AKI. Lerolle et al. [37]used RRI for the first time to predict the prognosis of critically ill patients and discovered that whether the occurrence or progression of AKI presents on the 5th day after septic shock was associated with a first day RRI of >0.74, and is not related with the presence or severity of AKI on day 1 [37]. A series of subsequent studies found that patients with an RRI of >0.70 had 29.85 times increased risk of persistent AKI [47], which was an independent risk factor for renal function deterioration after 1 year in patients with chronic cardiac insufficiency [48]; an RRI of >0.77 in patients with AKI was associated with an increased risk of death [49]. An RRI of ≥0.80 at least 3 months after kidney transplantation was closely related to graft dysfunction and mortality [50].

### Renal vein assessment

#### Method of obtaining the renal venous waveform

The method of obtaining the renal venous waveform is like that of renal artery assessment, but slightly different because the renal vein is highly compliant and susceptible to respiration. Therefore, the selection of 3 end-expiratory spectrum samples in the same respiratory cycle is recommended especially when taking deep breaths.

#### Renal venous waveform pattern and VII

Renal venous waveform has two types: continuous (patterns A, B, and C) and discontinuous (patterns D, E, and F). VII is a measure of vein pulsatility and is calculated based on the Doppler waveform: maximum velocity minus minimum velocity divided by maximum velocity. A normal waveform is continuous (pattern A) with a certain pulsatility change with a VII of 0.12–0.52 (Figure 5A). Pattern B (Figure 5B) and pattern C (Figure 5C) demonstrate a continuous waveform with either too small or too large pulsatility; these patterns are often found in abnormal waveforms and prone to progress to a discontinuous spectrum, although both can be observed in individuals with a normal kidney function. The discontinuous patterns are abnormal. Interruption or reversal of the end-diastolic blood flow indicates a pattern D (Figure 5D). Interruption or reversal both end-systolic blood flow and end-diastolic blood flow indicates a biphasic pattern E (Figure 5E); meanwhile, a blood flow that only appears during systole or diastole indicates a monophasic pattern (pattern F) (Figure 5F).

#### Renal vein waveform and VII generation principle and influencing factors

Unlike the arterial side, the vascular resistance on the venous side is normally negligible because the veins act as capacitance vessels; therefore, their impedance to blood flow is directly related to compliance. When the renal tissue compliance drops, the amplitude changes occurring throughout the cardiac cycle are suppressed, for example urinary tract obstructive nephropathy [51] (Figure 6A) and diabetic nephropathy [52] (Figure 5B).

*Figure 6.: Amplitude changes in renal venous blood flow waveform in the different renal interstitial pressure. A 46-year-old female patient with stable circulation and normal renal function 1 day after bilateral ovary and tumor resection. The right kidney (A) shows hydronephrosis, while the left kidney (B) is morphologically normal. The waveforms of the interlobar veins in both kidneys showed both continuous and intermittent end-diastolic interruption patterns, and the blood flow velocity and amplitude of the right interlobar veins were lower than those of the left kidney because of the relative higher right renal interstitial pressure. The higher amplitude of the interlobar vein of the left kidney is induced by the relative increased blood perfusion and unchanged interstitial pressure.*

Also because of the high compliance, the blood flow waveform of renal veins is significantly affected by the right atrium pressure (RAP) during a cardiac cycle [52]. Therefore, the normal renal vein waveform is not only continuous, but also changes with the variation of RAP during the cardiac cycle with a VII value between 0.12 and 0.52 (Figure 5A). The increase of RAP leads to the obstruction of renal venous return, and the waveform is interrupted or even reversed, which is most likely to occur in the atrial systole period (Figure 5D). If the pressure is further increased, the back flow is obstructed during the atrial systole and atrial filling periods, and it is manifested as a biphasic waveform (Figure 5E), or even only during the systole or diastolic period, and it is manifested as a uniphasic waveform (Figure 5F), mostly during the diastolic period.

The renal venous flow pattern ultimately depends on the combined effect of RAP and renal tissue compliance.

#### Clinical application of renal vein waveform and VII

Similarly, a comprehensive understanding of the principles and influencing factors of renal vein waveform and VII is the basic prerequisite for their appropriate clinical application, and the empirical application of these factors often leads to unsatisfactory clinical results.

#### Identify the etiologies

Due to the high compliance characteristics of the renal vein, it is highly sensitive to its influencing factors, and the renal vein waveform changes even earlier than that of CVP and the inferior vena cava [53]. Any factors that result in RAP elevation such as fluid overload, tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, or right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, would lead to the obstruction of the renal venous return.

Similarly, any factors that lead to decreased renal compliance such as CKD, diabetes [52] (Figure 5B), urinary tract obstruction [51, 54] (Figure 6A), renal tissue inflammation, and even the interlobar vein due to the relative lower compliance of the renal parenchyma in the normal kidney compared to the renal segmental vein due to relative higher compliance of the collecting system (Figure 5D) would lead to a decrease in the renal venous pulsatility; any factors that can lead to an increase in renal tissue compliance, such as decreased renal perfusion (Figure 6B) and the renal segmental vein in the normal kidney compared to the interlobar vein (Figure 5E).

#### RRT management

Discontinuous renal venous spectrum and increased VII indicates renal venous congestion, which suggests the renal response to diuretics is likely to be reduced; hence, these patients may benefit from RRT along with other indications for RRT and a higher dehydration rate. In patients with normal VII value and continuous renal venous spectrum, dehydration should be cautiously performed to prevent systemic instability; this event can also be an indication to stop RRT during an RRT aiming to dehydration.

#### Predict prognosis

The current studies mainly focuse on the prognosis of patients with heart failure [55–57] or recovering from cardiac surgery [58,59]. The discontinuous renal venous waveform is an ultrasonic index for venous congestion in patients with cardiac dysfunction [55–59], and an independent risk factor for poor prognosis such as readmission, heart transplantation, AKI [58,59] and mortality in patients with heart failure [55–57] or post cardiac surgery [58,59]; it is independent from RAP and serum atrial natriuretic peptide levels [55]. In addition, the risk for poor prognosis increases as the degree of venous congestion increases [8,57–59].

## Contrast-enhanced ultrasound and evaluation

Contrast Enhanced UltraSound (CEUS) is selectively applied according to the needs of illness and the capacity of the department.

After the above ultrasound examination, a final evaluation should be finished.

### CEUS

Renal perfusion alterations, especially at the microvascular level, appear to play a crucial role in AKI occurrence [10]. However, despite optimization of macrovascular hemodynamic parameters, occult renal hypoperfusion may persist with an early AKI [60]. On the other hand, after initial hemodynamic resuscitation, renal function impairment may also occur despite a preserved global RBF [61–66]. Hence, the assessment of the microcirculation alterations is necessary. The waveform of interlobar arteries and veins and the corresponding RRI and VII are usually used to evaluate the resistance of forward perfusion and back flow of renal microcirculation, indirectly reflecting microcirculation perfusion, but the consistency relationship between the two is affected by the complexity of AKI [64].

The development of ultrasound contrast media and the corresponding software for contrast quantification has opened possibilities for novel and noninvasive means of measuring perfusion directly [62–66]. Ultrasound contrast consists of microbubbles, which remain entirely intravascular throughout their lifespan and are not affected by glomerular filtration or tubular transport [66]. The bubbles have rheology and a size like that of red blood cells and are used for perfusion analysis in various organs. During CEUS, the use of intravenous contrast product increases the blood echogenicity and enhances the visualization of microcirculatory renal perfusion during an ultrasound examination. A good correlation was observed between CEUS measurements and gold standard renal blood flow measurements (para-aminohippurate clearance) [67].

#### Examination method

#### Common indicators

The quantitative indicators reflect the volume of microcirculation blood perfusion and blood flow velocity in microcirculation, including mechanical index, region of interest (ROI), acoustic intensity (AI), microvascular blood volume (MBV), microvascular blood flow (MBF), microvascular flow velocity (MFV), rise time (RT), wash in slope (WIS), time to peak (TTP), mean transit time (MTT), peak intensity (PI), time-intensity curves (TIC), and area under the curve (AUC). PI, AUC, and MBV reflect the volume of microcirculatory perfusion. RT, TTP, MTT, WIS, and MFV reflect the blood flow velocity in the microcirculation.

#### Contrast agent infusion mode

CEUS can be performed using a continuous microbubble infusion or by injection of a single bolus [68] (Figure 7).

Continuous microbubble infusion results in a steady state microbubble concentration (Figure 7A). A SonoVue dose of 2.4 mL/bottle is often selected and pumped at a rate of 1 mL/min after dilution with an equal amount of normal saline. Bolus administration (Figure 7B) produces a rapid increase in the contrast agent concentration and signal followed by a slower contrast washout and is the most common form of contrast agent administration for nondestructive imaging. A bolus injection should be immediately followed by the administration of 5–10 mL saline bolus to flush the line at the same speed at which the contrast agent was infused. High pressure should be avoided because it may lead to the destruction of microbubbles.

#### Clinical application

CEUS has the potential to allow clinicians to see the renal perfusion real-time, allowing rapid assessment of the efficacy of therapeutic interventions in individual patients at bedside.

For example, the perfusion indexes such as PI and AUC were decreased, while the perfusion pressure (MAP-CVP) and CO were normal or even higher than normal, indicating that the precapillary arteriole was more likely to shrink if combined with increased RRI; it is more likely to be associated with inflammation, strong stressors or high levels of vasopressors. At this time, MAP should be titrated by adjusting the dose of vasopressors according to PI and AUC, and strategies can be adopted to reduce inflammation and stress level, such as optimizing analgesic and sedation strategies. If combined with discontinuous renal vein waveform, which indicates that the renal microcirculation stasis induced by increased renal afterload may play a certain role in it, and CVP should be reduced simultaneously or first. While, if the decreased perfusion was associated with insufficient perfusion pressure or CO, the causes of insufficient MAP and CO should be found and resolved, and then renal microcirculation perfusion should be evaluated again.

Microcirculation blood flow velocity is generally a sensitive indicator reflecting microcirculation perfusion. Patients with early sepsis generally show increased blood flow velocity and decreased RT and MTT. If RT and MTT and other indicators are prolonged, it indicates the possibility of vasoconstriction regardless of the PI and AUC.

Of note, although the prominent role of the CEUS, the use of it to guide renal perfusion resuscitation needs further investigation.

### Evaluation

Evaluation means interpreting ultrasound results and integrating them with clinical information to make clinical judgments and treatment decisions. Evaluation is dynamic and continuous and should be conducted during each step throughout the whole protocol. At the end of the protocol, a final comprehensive evaluation is required.

## Advantages of CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol

First, this protocol is the first protocol to use bedside ultrasound to comprehensively evaluate renal hemodynamics. Each step contains a rich connotation of the critical illness, which presents the renal tissue structure and renal blood perfusion, morphology and function, physiology and pathology, medical history and etiology in front of the clinicians continuously and dynamically. Second, this protocol has noninvasive, convenient, real-time, dynamic, and economical features, thus enabling individualized and organ-target diagnosis and treatment at the bedside. At last, this protocol is an example of the organic integration of critical care medicine and POCUS, which was completed under the guidance of the principle of critical illness.

## Disadvantages

First, the completion of this protocol requires solid basic skills of critical ultrasound and profound knowledge of pathophysiology. Incorrect acquisition and interpretation of ultrasound sections will lead to incorrect clinical judgment. However, this is true of every laboratory examination and monitoring technique.

And there is still a lack of research data to support the efficacy of the CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol; our clinical randomized trial on this protocol is still in progress at the moment, and a large-scale of sample, multi-center clinical randomized trial will be conducted in the future.

## Conclusion

The CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE procedure is a bedside ultrasound examination that examines the morphology and blood flow of the kidneys. Combined with the patient’s current and past medical history, this method can be used for comprehensive evaluation of the renal hemodynamics and acquisition and analysis of the pathophysiological mechanisms of the occurrence and progression of AKI; therefore, the occurrence and progression of AKI can be predicted, and targeted, individualized AKI diagnosis and treatment based on the pathophysiological mechanisms can be implemented; such management strategy should be promoted and implemented in the clinical setting.

# Establishment of a TaqMan-based real-time quantitative PCR method for detection of exogenous fowl adenovirus type Ⅰ, type Ⅲ and avian leukosis virus in human cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines

**Authors:** Min Wu; Baihui Zhi; Rui Sheng; Entong Zhou; Qian Zhou; Jiemin Li; Xiaoshu Fu; Yanchun Wu; Yunchang Zhang; Pingjie Sun; Wei Jia; Liang Shi; Dawei Liu; Hui Zhao; Weiheng Su

**Affiliations:** aNational Engineering Laboratory for AIDS Vaccine, School of Life Sciences, Jilin University, Changchun, 130012, China | bBCHT Biotechnology Company, Changchun, 130012, China | cBeijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Company, Beijing, 100012, China | dNational Institutes for Food and Drug Control, Beijing, 102629, China | eKey Laboratory for Molecular Enzymology and Engineering of the Ministry of Education, School of Life Sciences, Jilin University, Changchun, 130012, China

## Abstract

Cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines can effectively prevent human disease and death caused by influenza virus. Since chicken embryos are used as the culture substrate for the large-scale production of influenza vaccines, cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines may be contaminated by exogenous avian viruses. Rapid and sensitive methods such as TaqMan-based quantitative PCR are needed for the detection of exogenous avian viruses during cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines production. In this study, a TaqMan-based quantitative PCR method was established for the detection of three common exogenous avian viruses, including fowl adenovirus type I, type Ⅲ and avian leukosis virus. Avian virus-encoding plasmids purified in high-performance liquid chromatography were essential for sensitivity analysis. The sensitivity reached 1 copy per reaction for each of the avian virus plasmids. Standard curves showed a strong linear relationship. The TaqMan-based quantitative PCR method had high specificity and no cross-reactivity with other irrelevant viruses. Furthermore, the established TaqMan-based quantitative PCR can effectively detect 0.1 TCID50 of each avian virus without or with interference from the influenza virus nucleic acid. Ultimately, this method was used to test three master seed lots of monovalent cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccine, and the results showed that no fowl adenovirus type I, type Ⅲ or avian leukosis virus contamination, which were consistent with serological methods. The TaqMan-based quantitative PCR method for the determination of extraneous avian viruses in cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines met the requirement for both conventional and emergency inspection on cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines.

Keywords: Cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines (CA-LAIVs), Exogenous avian virus, Fowl adenovirus type Ⅰ (FAdV Ⅰ), Fowl adenovirus type Ⅲ (FAdV Ⅲ), Avian leukosis virus (ALV), TaqMan-based quantitative PCR (qPCR)

## Abstract

TaqMan-qPCR was established for detection of FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV in human CA-LAIVs.

TaqMan-qPCR method showed appropriate linearity and high specificity.

The sensitivity of TaqMan-qPCR method was 1 gene copy or 1 TCID50 per reaction.

QPCR detected no avian virus in master seed lots of CA-LAIV, same as serologic tests.

## Introduction

Influenza viruses have always been a major threat to human health. The World Health Organization estimates that 290,000–650,000 people die each year from respiratory diseases related to seasonal influenza [[1], [2], [3]]. Vaccination has always been the first choice for flu prevention [4,5]. Nasal-spray cold adapted live attenuated influenza vaccines (CA-LAIVs) are an important constituent of marketed influenza vaccines for humans, due to their highly effective and durable immunogenicity in inducing mucosal, cellular, and humoral immunity, and non-invasive vaccination method [[6], [7], [8], [9], [10]]. Both CA-LAIVs and inactivated influenza vaccines mainly rely on chicken embryos as a proliferation media in industrial production. A large number of chicken embryos are used in the preparation process of influenza vaccine. However, these may carry or be infected with exogenous avian viruses, which can lead to contamination and safety concerns for the influenza vaccines.

Fowl adenovirus types Ⅰ (FAdV Ⅰ), types Ⅲ (FAdV Ⅲ) and avian leukosis virus (ALV) are three common exogenous avian viruses that contaminate chicken embryos [[11], [12], [13]]. FAdVs, a type of DNA virus, are pathogens in poultry and wild birds and can be divided into three groups (Ⅰ−Ⅲ) according to the clinical symptoms and host range [14,15]. FAdV Ⅰ can be divided into 12 serotypes (1–8a, 8b–11) [16]. Serotype 1 (FAdV-1), also known as the chick embryo lethal orphan virus, circulates broadly in chickens and mainly causes chicken gizzard erosion [16,17]. The Chinese Pharmacopoeia recommends testing for FAdV-1 when vaccine was produced in chicken embryos. FAdV Ⅲ, also named egg drop syndrome virus, mainly replicates in the oviduct of poultry and forms a basophilic inclusion body after infection, which causes eggshell abnormalities, egg body deformity, and a decrease in egg production [18,19]. There is only one serotype identified within FAdV Ⅲ [15]. ALV, an RNA virus, is classified into subgroups A–J [20]. The subgroups A-E and J of ALV were isolated from chickens while other subgroups (F–I) only infected pheasants [21]. Subgroups J and A are the most commonly identified ALV in China [12]. ALV can infect chickens and causes a variety of neoplasms, including lymphoid and myeloid leukoses [22]. Due to tumor mortality and low growth rate in infected chickens, egg production is decreased in hens who contract ALV [23]. These three viruses cause serious economic losses in the poultry industry worldwide. Since CA-LAIVs are based on live influenza virus, FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV must be detected in the master seed lot of CA-LAIVs to ensure the safety of the vaccines production.

Traditional serological method for the detection of exogenous avian virus mainly relies on virus isolation [24,25]. However, there are disadvantages to these methods, such as complicated experimental operation processes and long detection periods. Improving the efficiency and accuracy of exogenous virus contamination detection has become essential in the field of biological product safety in recent years. The TaqMan-based real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) method can be a quick (within 1 day) detection method for viruses within biological products. TaqMan-based qPCR has higher sensitivity and specificity than conventional qPCR technology and serological method, and it also has high throughput and low pollution characteristics [25,26].

In this study, we explored and established a TaqMan-based qPCR method for exogenous FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV in the master seed lot of CA-LAIVs to improve detection sensitivity and efficiency to meet the requirements of rapid detection of human CA-LAIVs.

## Materials and methods

### Virus strains and cell lines

FAdV Ⅰ, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV were purchased from the China National Institute of Veterinary Drug Control. Three master seed lots of CA-LAIVs, including A/17/Darwin/2018/154 (H1N1, batch number MH1N12020002), A/17/Hong Kong/2019/2573 (H3N2, batch number MH3N22020001), and B/60/Washington/2019/3676 (batch number MB2020001) were produced in BCHT Biotechnology Company (Changchun, China). Mouse adenovirus type Ⅰ (MAdV Ⅰ), human adenovirus type Ⅴ (HAdV Ⅴ), and attenuated influenza viruses, including A/17/Darwin/2018/154 (H1N1), A/17/Hong Kong/2019/2573 (H3N2), and B/60/Washington/2019/3676, were from laboratory storage. Chicken embryo liver cells (CEL) and chicken embryo fibroblasts (CEF) were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC; Manassas, VA, USA).

### Preparation of standard plasmids

According to the viral genome sequences of FAdV Ⅰ (GenBank number MK050972.1), FAdV Ⅲ (GenBank number Y09598.1) and ALV (GenBank number AB112960.1), three sequences were selected as the target genes: FAdV Ⅰ (in Fiber 1 gene region of FAdV-1): CGCTTACTGCCGTTTAGCTGCTGCAGGTGGCGTGGTCAGCGGGACCATTCAAGTGACAAGCTATGCC (67 bp), FAdV Ⅲ (in endopeptidase gene region): TGTGTCACATTAATCCCTTTGAAGCTTCTATATTTCAAGCTATGCATGGTACCTCCCCGGCTTTGTATCCTTCCAAACCTCATCTGTTGC (90 bp), and ALV (in 3’ untranslated regions (UTR) which sequence is relatively conserved among ALV subgroups [27,28]): ATCGTGGTATGATCGTGCCTTATTAGGAAGGCAACAGACGGGTCTGACATGGATTGGACGAACTC (65 bp). The target DNA of the three avian viruses were synthesized and inserted into the PMD19-T vector by Sangon Biotech Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) were performed for plasmid purification. Plasmid concentration was measured using the NanoDrop-3000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), and the plasmids were then diluted to the indicated copies/μL according to the following formula [29]: plasmid dilution (copies/μL) = (6.02 × 1023 × plasmid concentration (ng/μL)/(genome length × 109 × 650).

### Preparation of FAdV Ⅰ, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV

CEL and CEF were incubated with Basal Medium Eagle (BME) or Medium 199 (M − 199) with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA) in T25 flasks at 37 °C and 5 % CO2 before the experiment. When the cell density reached approximately 80 %, CEL was inoculated with purchased FAdV I or FAdV Ⅲ with multiplicity of infection (MOI) = 0.1, and CEF was inoculated with purchased ALV with MOI = 0.1 in serum-free medium at 37 °C for 1 h. The CEL and CEF were washed with PBS and cultured in BME or M − 199 medium supplemented with 2 % FBS at 37 °C. The supernatant was collected at 3 days post infection (dpi) for FAdV Ⅰ and FAdV Ⅲ or 5 dpi for ALV and could be immediately used for subsequent nucleic acid extraction or stored at −80 °C.

### Infectivity titration of FAdV Ⅰ, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV by 50 % tissue culture infectious dose (TCID50) assay

CEL and CEF were seeded in 96-well culture plates and incubated with BME or M − 199 medium with 10 % FBS (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA) at 37 °C and 5 % CO2 for 24 h. Then, the supernatant was removed and 50 μL of 10-fold serially diluted FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ or ALV was added, respectively. After incubation for 1 h, inoculates were removed and replaced with medium with 2 % FBS. The infected cells were incubated at 37 °C and 5 % CO2 for 3 days (FAdV I and FAdV Ⅲ) or 7 days (ALV). The appearance of cytopathic effect (CPE) was monitored in each well of the plate, and the viral TCID50 titers were calculated using the Reed and Muench method.

### Viral nucleic acid extraction and reverse transcription

CA-LAIVs and influenza viruses were inactivated at 56 °C for 30 min. CA-LAIVs, influenza viruses, FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ, ALV, MAdV Ⅰ, and HAdV Ⅴ viral nucleic acid were extracted using the PureLink™ Viral RNA/DNA Mini Kit (Invitrogen, Carslbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The extracted CA-LAIV RNA, influenza virus RNA or ALV RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the TransScript®Ⅱ One-Step gDNA Removal and cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (TransGen Biotech Co., Ltd., Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

### TaqMan-based real-time qPCR

One microliter of DNA or cDNA of each sample was mixed with 10 μL 2 × premix Ex Taq, 0.5 μL forward primer (10 μ mol L−1), 0.5 μL reverse primer (10 μ mol L−1), 0.25 μL probe (10 μ mol L−1), and 7.75 μL nuclease-free water for the TaqMan-based qPCR using the TaqMan™ Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The primers and probes for the three avian viruses (Table 1) were synthesized by the Sangon Biotech Company. Subsequently, two qPCR procedures were performed using the QuantStudio™ 5 qPCR instrument (Applied Biosystems), using the following procedures: (i) the standard procedure, whereby the mixture was pre-denatured at 50 °C for 2 min and 95 °C for 10 min, followed by amplification for 40 cycles at 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 1 min; and (ii) the fast procedure, whereby the mixture was pre-denatured at 50 °C for 2 min and 95 °C for 30 s, followed by amplification for 40 cycles at 95 °C for 5 s and 60 °C for 30 s.

| FAdV Ⅲ | 5′-TGTGTCACATTAATCCCTTTGAAGCT-3′ | 5′-GCAACAGATGAGGTTTGGAAGGATA-3′ | 5′-(FAM)-TACCTCCCCGGCTTTG-(BHQ-1 or MGB)-3′ |

For the sensitivity analysis of the TaqMan-based qPCR, standard plasmids of FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ or ALV was diluted to 1–101 copy μL−1 as DNA templates for TaqMan-based qPCR amplification (10 reactions for each dilution). Nuclease-free water was used as the negative control. The sensitivity of the method was determined by the minimum dilution ratio with a positive detection rate of 10/10. The sensitivity experiment was repeated thrice.

To establish the TaqMan-based qPCR standard curves, standard plasmids of FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ or ALV were diluted 10-fold (107-1 copies μL−1) as DNA template for TaqMan-based qPCR amplification. Each dilution level was duplicated, and nuclease-free water was used as the negative control. With copy number as the abscissa and Ct value as the ordinate, the standard curve (107–103 copies per reaction) was generated to obtain the regression equation. R2 ≥ 0.99 was considered qualified. The reaction efficiency was determined automatically by using QuantStudio™ Design and Analysis Software v1.5.1 (Applied Biosystems). The standard curve experiment was repeated thrice.

### Detection for FAdV I using agar gel precipitation (AGP)

Firstly, commercial HA serums for neutralizion of LAIVs were prepared. Briefly, sheep anti-influenza A/Guangdong-Maonan/SWL/1536/2019-like (H1N1, the same HA as attenuated strain A/17/Darwin/2018/154) HA serum, sheep anti-influenza A/HongKong/2671/2019-like (H3N2, the same HA as attenuated strain A/17/Hong Kong/2019/2573) HA serum, and sheep anti-influenza B/Washington/02/2019-Like (B Victoria Lineage, the same HA as attenuated strain B/60/Washington/2019/3676) HA serum (all obtained from NIBSC, England) were treated with receptor-destroying enzyme (RDE) at a ratio of 1:4 and incubated at 37 °C for 18 h. The RDE-treated serum was then inactivated at 56 °C for 30 min. Next, three master seed lots of CA-LAIVs (H1N1, H3N2, and IBV) were neutralized completely with an equal volume (500 μL) of homologous anti- HA serum at 33 °C for 1 h.

The neutralized CA-LAIV was inoculated into 80 % confluent CEL and cultured for 3 days. The supernatant was separated after freeze-thawing and passaged twice in fresh CEL. The culture supernatant from each passage of the three samples was mixed with (NH4)2SO4 at 4 °C overnight. After centrifugation, the sediment was dissolved in PBS. Twenty-five microliters of FAdV I positive serum (Beijing North Weiye Institute of Measuring and Testing Technology, Beijing, China) was added in the central well of agar gel, and 25 μL samples of each passage was added to the surrounding wells and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. The results were regarded positive when a clear specific precipitation line between the samples and the positive serum well was observed; otherwise, they were deemed negative. Cell-cultured FAdV I and BME medium served as the positive and negative controls, respectively. The AGP assay was repeated thrice.

### Detection for FAdV Ⅲ using HA assay

The neutralized master seed lot of CA-LAIV was inoculated into CEL and cultured for 3 days. The supernatant was collected from each of the three continuous passages. Fifty microliters of culture supernatants of each passage were diluted from 2° to 2−12 in a two-fold gradient. Then, 50 μL of 1 % chicken red blood cell suspension was added, and the samples were incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The results were regarded positive if erythrocyte agglutination was observed; otherwise, they were deemed negative. The inverse of the maximum dilution at which hemagglutination occurred was considered as the HA titer of samples. Cell-cultured FAdV Ⅲ and BME medium served as the positive and negative controls, respectively. The HA assay was repeated thrice.

### Detection of ALV using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

The neutralized master seed lot of CA-LAIV was inoculated into CEF and cultured for 7 days. The supernatant was collected from each of the three continuous passages. The culture supernatants of each passage were examined using the ALV Antigen Test Kit (IDEXX Laboratories Co. Ltd., Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions (n = 3). Cell-cultured ALV and M − 199 were used as the positive and negative controls, respectively. The optical density (OD) was determined at 630 nm using the iMarkTM Microplate Reader (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). The experiment was considered valid when the OD value of negative control was < 0.150 and that of the positive control was > 0.200. The ratio of the sample with the positive control (S/P) was calculated using the following formula:

$$ S/P = (mean ODsample – mean ODnegative control) / (mean ODpositive control – mean ODnegative control) $$

S/P > 0.2 was noted positive and S/P ≤ 0.2 negative. The ELISA assay was repeated three times.

### Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using GraphPad Prism v7 (GraphPad, San Diego, CA, USA). Data represent mean ± standard deviation (SD) (n = 3). The standard curve formula and R2 are calculated by QuantStudio™ Design and Analysis Software v1.5.1 (Applied Biosystems). The coefficient of variation (CV) is calculated by the followed formula: CV = (SD/mean) × 100.

## Results

### Optimization for the sensitivity of the TaqMan-based qPCR assay for FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV

To develop a sensitive and stable TaqMan-based qPCR method to ensure the detection of the three common exogenous avian viruses in CA-LAIVs, we performed the following experiments: to explore the impact of different factors on sensitivity, we tested 1) plasmid templates purified using different methods; 2) different quenched groups of probes; 3) different qPCR procedures; and 4) different qPCR 8-tubes to conduct the following experiment.

First, plasmids encoding FAdV Ⅰ, purified using PAGE or HPLC, were used as templates in the QuantStudio™ 5 qPCR instrument. The plasmids, purified using PAGE, did not show great sensitivity, with a maximum detection of 3/10 amplification curves at 101 copies per reaction and 2/10 amplification curves at 1 copy per reaction (Table 2). Likewise, plasmids of FAdV Ⅲ and ALV did not reach the 10/10 sensitivity standard when purified using PAGE (data not shown). However, plasmids purified using HPLC had excellent sensitivity, with a detection of 10/10 amplification curves at both 101 copies per reaction and 1 copy per reaction (Table 2).

To verify the reproducibility of the sensitivity for the TaqMan based qPCR, the sensitivity experiment was repeated thrice for each type of plasmid purified using HPLC. Results showed that 10/10 sensitivity curve can be obtained at 101 and 1 copy per reaction, indicating a strong repeatability and stability of the TaqMan based qPCR.

Next, to explore if other conditions in the qPCR process can impact sensitivity, FAdV Ⅰ plasmids purified using HPLC were used for the experiment. We found that other factors, including different quenched groups of probes (MGB or FHQ-1), different procedures (standard or fast), and different consumables (white or transparent qPCR 8-tube) had almost no effect on sensitivity, and the 10/10 curves could be detected at both 101 and 1 copy per reaction (Table 2).

Ultimately, we found that plasmid purity was an essential factor in sensitivity, and the TaqMan-based qPCR assay with the detection limit of 1 copy per reaction was established for FAdV I (Fig. 1A), FAdV Ⅲ (Fig. 1B) and ALV (Fig. 1C).

### Establishment of the linear range of the TaqMan-based qPCR assay for FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV

To determine the appropriate linear range of TaqMan-based qPCR, standard plasmids was diluted from 107 to 1 copies per reaction for amplification for FAdV I (Fig. 2A), FAdV Ⅲ (Fig. 2B) or ALV (Fig. 2C). The standard curve is shown in Fig. 3. This assay showed a good linear relationship over a 107–103 copies per reaction range. The R2 values obtained for FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ, and ALV were 0.999 (Figs. 3A), 0.999 (Fig. 3B) and 0.999 (Fig. 3C), respectively. Additionally, the reaction efficiencies were determined to be 95.71 %, 97.56 %, and 95.63 % for FAdV I, FAdV Ⅲ and ALV, respectively.
